page: Vultr vx1-m-4c-32gb is a memory-optimized virtual server belonging to the VX1 Cloud Compute family. It features 4 dedicated vCPUs mapped to 2 physical AMD EPYC cores with 2 threads per core, operating at a base clock speed of 2.0 GHz. The processor architecture is x86_64, supported by 48 KB L1d cache, 1.0 MB L2 cache, and 32 MB L3 cache. The system is equipped with 32.0 GB of system memory, yielding a high memory-to-core ratio of 8.0 GB per vCPU. Local storage is limited to a 1 GB network-attached volume, and there are no onboard GPUs.

Performance benchmarks indicate strong single-core capabilities. The server achieves top-tier status in stress-ng single-core CPU performance, single-threaded gzip compression, and single-threaded bzip3 decompression. Geekbench single-core testing also registers a strong score. However, multi-core scaling is more moderate, with stress-ng multi-core performance, Geekbench multi-core, and PassMark CPU scores falling into the average tier. Multi-threaded bzip3 decompression is relatively weak, landing in the bottom 25%. Memory bandwidth tests for both cached and uncached reads and writes consistently place in the average range.

For specialized workloads, the AMD EPYC processor supports advanced instruction sets including AVX-512 (VNNI and BF16) and cryptography standards like AES and SHA_NI. In database and web serving benchmarks, the instance delivers average performance, processing 8.06 million Redis SET operations per second and maintaining a static web serving throughput of 14.6 GB/sec. Large language model inference is average for small 135M models but drops to poor for prompt processing on medium 7B models.

Given the high memory allocation relative to the vCPU count, this server offers qualitative cost efficiency for memory-intensive applications that do not require massive parallel processing power. It is well-suited for caching layers, relational database hosting, text processing pipelines, and lightweight web serving. The lack of substantial local storage means workloads requiring high-speed local disk I/O must rely on external network storage solutions.
